extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (including entry-level applicants, in-house communicators, and PR managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on professional status, ethical conduct, career success traits, and the organizational role and management responsibilities of public relations within organizations. Covers required skills, managerial access, relationships with outside counsel, and top-management obligations for effective PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Many public relations practitioners qualify as 'professionals' on the basis of their commitment to meeting professional and ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic criteria (status vs occupational professionalism) are noted; enduring professional values include personal service, a dislike of competition/advertising/profit, belief in payment-for-work principle, and the superiority of service motives. Professionalism is an important concern and goal for those entering the emerging profession of public relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes of ethics and individual behavior signal professional status; practitioners must choose to behave ethically or unethically, and those choices affect clients, employers, and the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upholding the highest ethical standards is core to improving the field's reputation. Practical implication: individuals should work to 'earn and nurture the respect' of clients, media, and the public, and organizations should support ethical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key competencies for success (executive survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top PR executives identify communication skills, knowledge of media and management, problem-solving abilities, motivation, and intellectual curiosity as needed for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These broad competencies form the baseline expectations employers have for effective PR practitioners and can guide hiring and professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results (Richard Long: 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reputation for getting results; being goal oriented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers and clients pay for results, not for effort alone. Career advancement depends on demonstrable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualizing (Richard Long: 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to focus on the employer’s or client’s needs; being a quick study, a good listener, and a thorough note taker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong conceptualizers understand organizational goals and translate them into communication strategy; listening and rapid comprehension are key skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Relations (Richard Long: 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Team players who balance personal goals with organizational goals and know how to deal with management, including when they disagree with the boss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpersonal competence and political savvy matter in organizations; career success requires navigating relationships effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style (Richard Long: 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'can-do' attitude and constructive competitiveness; translating confidence into persuasive advocacy and substantive PR contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style-related traits affect how others perceive PR practitioners' readiness for higher responsibility; attitude and persuasive presence are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intangibles (Richard Long: 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charisma, presence, and moxie—qualities that almost defy description but affect managerial evaluation of PR people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits influence promotion and perceived leadership potential despite being hard to quantify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing ability (primary skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write grammatically correct, easy-to-read, forceful, informative, and persuasive copy for publication and speech in both traditional and digital formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executives rank writing as the single most important skill for entry-level and long-term success; weak writing is repeatedly cited as a major deficiency in graduates. Practitioners should prioritize developing strong writing skills before advancing in their careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional employer-sought traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding of how the business works, skills with computer software and new media technology, being well read and informed on current events, ability to deal with frustration and stress, and ability to improvise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers look beyond communication skills to business acumen, technical literacy, general knowledge, resilience, and adaptability; include these in hiring criteria and professional development plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate accountability through measurable results
rubrics_metrics.description: To remain on the management team, public relations must contribute to achieving organizational goals and demonstrate accountability through measurable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR functions should set clear metrics, report outcomes, and align activities with organizational objectives to earn and retain executive-level influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top management commitment and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Top management must show commitment to and participation in public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR effectiveness depends on visible executive support; without it, PR credibility and influence are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of competent public relations counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Top management should retain competent public relations counsel (internal or external).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent counsel—internal or outside—ensures skilled handling of communication tasks and crises; management should prioritize hiring or engaging qualified PR professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of PR perspectives in policy making
rubrics_metrics.description: Top management must incorporate public relations perspectives in policy making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrating communication considerations into policy decisions helps avoid reputation risks and ensures coherent external messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way communication with internal and external publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Management should support two-way communication with both internal and external publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogic communication builds trust and informs decision making; PR should facilitate listening as well as message delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of actions and messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordination of what is done with what is said (alignment between actions and communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepancies between behavior and messages damage credibility; PR must ensure consistency across actions, policies, and public statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly defined goals and objectives for PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Top management should establish clearly defined goals and objectives for public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear goals enable measurement, accountability, and alignment with organizational strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management integrity and social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations credibility derives substantially from the behavior, integrity, and socially responsible actions of senior officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies (Perrier, BP, Tepco, Johnson & Johnson) illustrate that executive honesty, prompt action prioritizing safety, and social responsibility shape public trust more than PR efforts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand line vs. staff roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is typically a staff function that advises and supports line managers who have authority to run the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must understand the advisory nature of staff roles; the distinction affects reporting lines, authority, and expectations. Awareness of this helps PR align work with line managers' responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earned participation in management (proximity and access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in policy setting and decision making is earned; proximity and access to senior management increase PR's participation in management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices that increase access (physical proximity, informal contact, trusted relationships) help PR gain influence. Being seen as a vital member of the dominant coalition (senior decision-makers) grows PR power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage client–agency relationships when retaining outside counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Client–firm relationships typically involve retainer fees, coverage of set hours, billing for extra work, collaboration between firm account executives and internal staff, and potential friction over availability and invoicing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear agreements about retainer scope, billing, project responsibilities, and expectations reduce conflict; clients should recognize outside counsel as a variable cost with its own economic goals, and both sides should maintain open coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor PR structure to organizational circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal public relations departments are 'tailor-made' to fit a particular organization's unique circumstances and CEO expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one-size-fits-all structure exists; decisions about reporting lines, staffing, and functions should reflect organizational size, mission, external environment, and strategic priorities.
